{"model":"claude-fable-5-1","id":"msg_011CfK6RS7ZBcYb3RqQvFV16","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "The ferry at Sallow Crossing stopped running the spring Halvard turned sixty-one, and the letter from the county came the same week to say the new bridge downstream would carry the traffic now, inspected each season by engineers who arrived in a white truck. Halvard read it in the wheelhouse with the diesel still ticking as it cooled, then coiled the mooring lines the way he always had, though no one would need to be carried over again.

He still walked down to the landing at first light. There was nothing to ferry, but his ears knew the sound of the river rising after rain better than they knew his own kitchen, and the current did not seem to have heard that the crossing was closed. He would stand on the ramp as the mist lifted off the water, and the school bus would go over the bridge a mile down, small and yellow above the trees, and he would count the cars behind it the way his father had taught him to count fares.

The drivers said the bridge never waited and never turned anyone back for weather. He believed them. He still watched the far bank in the evenings, naming the farms by the shape of their barns, and once the Ostrander girl leaned on her horn from the bridge deck, which was either habit or kindness, and Halvard did not go up to the house.

What surprised him was how the town kept crossing without anyone to hold the cable for it. He had thought himself the way over. Now he understood he had mostly been the one who stood between the two banks and looked at both. The river had never needed his hand on the throttle; it had needed someone on the landing who believed each morning that the crossing mattered.
